headline: Testosterone’s label
just changed.
dek: FDA dropped the heart-risk boxed warning in 2025 and added a blood pressure warning.

paragraphs: On February 28, 2025, FDA told the makers of every [[/testosterone|testosterone]] product to change their labels. They were to add the results of a large heart-safety trial called TRAVERSE, remove Boxed Warning language about a higher risk of heart outcomes, and add or update warnings that testosterone can raise blood pressure. FDA said its blood pressure studies confirmed an increase across the class.

TRAVERSE was the largest trial behind that change. It enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with heart disease or high heart risk and low testosterone, and gave them a daily gel or a placebo gel, with mean follow-up of 33 months. Heart attack, stroke or heart death occurred in 7.0% of men on testosterone and 7.3% on placebo. Atrial fibrillation (3.5% vs 2.4%), acute kidney injury (2.3% vs 1.5%) and pulmonary embolism were more common on testosterone. A sub-study of 5,204 of the men found fractures in 3.50% on testosterone and 2.46% on placebo. The trial was built to test heart safety, not whether testosterone helps symptoms.

Some things did not change. FDA kept the label’s limit on age: safety and effectiveness in men whose testosterone is low only because of age have not been established, and use outside the labeled conditions is off-label. Testosterone stays a Schedule III controlled substance. The creams and sprays Adonis carries are compounded, and compounded drugs are not FDA approved. We could not confirm whether Adonis’s cypionate injections are the approved product or compounded.

The labels also say that testosterone from outside the body shuts down the brain’s signals to the testes, and at large doses can suppress sperm production. In a 1990 World Health Organization study of weekly injections as male contraception, 157 of 271 men stopped producing sperm; after injections stopped, the median time back to a normal count was 3.7 months.

That is the reason men ask about three other drugs in this lane. [[/enclomiphene|Enclomiphene]] is not approved anywhere we checked. The EU refused it in 2018, citing unproven benefit and a blood-clot risk that included one fatal stroke, and an FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 4 in 2022 against letting pharmacies compound it from bulk. It is still compounded while FDA evaluates it. [[/anastrozole|Anastrozole]] is approved only for breast cancer in postmenopausal women; in men it is off-label, and in a one-year trial in 88 older men spine bone density fell on it and rose on placebo.

The third, [[/hcg|hCG]], is approved for undescended testes in boys, some men with low testosterone from a pituitary problem, and ovulation in women. Using it alongside testosterone is off-label, and the studies of that use we found are small: 29 men for three weeks, and a review of 26 men’s records. Since March 23, 2020, hCG has been regulated as a biologic, which FDA says is not eligible for the usual compounding exemptions.

pull.quote: removing language from the Boxed Warning related to an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes for all testosterone products.
